name: OpenBao
summary: The open-source fork of HashiCorp Vault, kept under the MPL after Vault’s 2023 licence change: the same API, `bao` instead of `vault`, and namespaces without an enterprise licence.
intro: OpenBao works the way Vault does, because it started as a copy of Vault’s last MPL-licensed code. It is a server that keeps secrets encrypted in storage, starts sealed until enough Shamir key shares or a KMS unseal it, logs clients in through auth methods such as Kubernetes or OIDC, and hands out leased secrets: key-value data, short-lived database users, certificates from its PKI engine and encryption as a service from Transit. The project says its API should be compatible enough that existing Vault clients don’t notice the difference. Its migration guide moves a Vault 1.14.1 Community cluster on Raft storage; newer Vault versions and Vault Enterprise are untested, tokens take a shorter format, and fewer plugins are built in.

Since the fork, OpenBao has added features Vault keeps for its Enterprise edition or doesn’t have. Namespaces for multi-tenancy arrived in 2.3 in 2025, and 2.6 lets each namespace have its own seal. Since 2.5, standby nodes can serve reads, first on Raft storage and since 2.7 on PostgreSQL too, and 2.7, released on October 5, 2026, added ML-DSA and ML-KEM post-quantum algorithms. IBM engineers started the fork at LF Edge in December 2023; 2.0, the first GA release, followed in July 2024, and in June 2025 the project moved to the OpenSSF, where it is a sandbox project. GitLab is building its native CI secrets manager on it.
strengths: OSI open source under MPL 2.0 and neutral governance, so it can be embedded in products and offered as a service, which Vault’s Business Source License restricts
Close to a drop-in for Vault Community: the same API, auth methods and secrets engines, so most clients and integrations keep working
Namespaces and per-namespace seals at no cost, where Vault’s namespaces need Enterprise or HCP Vault Dedicated
Read scaling on standby nodes, with Raft or PostgreSQL as storage
limits: Migration from Vault is tested only from 1.14.1 Community; later Vault versions and Enterprise clusters are unsupported
Fewer plugins ship by default, and mounts whose plugin isn’t built in are skipped at startup until you deal with them
The same operational work as Vault: unsealing after restarts, a storage cluster, backups and upgrades
Still a sandbox project, the OpenSSF’s earliest stage, and reads from standby nodes can be slightly stale

worksWith.how: can keep its encrypted storage in

snippet.title: A namespace per team, addressed with the same API paths as Vault
source: bao namespace create team-a/                  # no enterprise licence needed
bao write team-a/sys/mounts/kv type=kv        # a KV engine inside the namespace

story: In August 2023 HashiCorp moved Vault from the Mozilla Public License to the Business Source License. Engineers at IBM working on Open Horizon, an LF Edge project, started a fork of the last MPL code, and in December 2023 it was announced as OpenBao, incubated at LF Edge with IBM developers leading it, though IBM had not officially endorsed it. EdgeX Foundry, another LF Edge project, later adopted it as its secret store.

OpenBao 2.0, the first GA release, came out in July 2024 and concentrated on stabilising the fork; it also dropped mlock and slimmed the binary. From 2025 the project began adding features Vault keeps for paying customers, starting with namespaces in 2.3. In June 2025 it moved from LF Edge to the OpenSSF, its technical steering committee saying the security foundation better matched its contributors and mission. In 2026 it added read scaling, per-namespace seals and post-quantum algorithms, reaching 2.7 in October.

choices.choice: Fork from the last open-source Vault
choices.why: Starting from MPL-licensed Vault 1.14 kept the API, clients and integrations people already used, so moving could be a migration of storage rather than a rewrite.
Existing clients, SDKs and tools that speak the Vault API, including the `X-Vault-Namespace` header, keep working, and namespaces follow Vault Enterprise’s model to ease migrations.

choices.choice: A smaller core, with integrations as plugins
choices.why: OpenBao ships fewer plugins in the binary and has moved integrations such as KMS auto-unseal and HSM-backed keys into external plugins, so they can be released on their own schedule, independent of the core.

timeline.text: HashiCorp relicenses Vault in August; OpenBao announced at LF Edge in December
OpenBao 2.0, the first GA release, in July
Namespaces in 2.3; moves to the OpenSSF as a sandbox project in June
Read scaling in 2.5; per-namespace seals in 2.6 in August; 2.7 on October 5
